pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: perform MENTAL calculations, including mixed operations and large numbers, using strategies such as partitioning, compensation and derived facts (flexible, fact-based mental methods).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'perform mental calculations, including with mixed operations and large numbers' and 'use their knowledge of the order of operations'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): the mental-strategy expectation is distributed — 3.OA.5 properties as strategies, 4.NBT.5/6 place-value & properties strategies, 5.NBT.6, and MP7 (structure) / MP8 (regularity) underpin flexible mental methods.
• Operational details — the child chooses an efficient mental route: partitioning (45×8 = 40×8 + 5×8 = 360), compensation (99×6 = 100×6 − 6), derived facts (knowing 6×4 to get 6.5×4), doubling/halving, and factorising. Mixed-operation strings (250×3 + 500) require applying order of operations mentally. The emphasis is on SELECTING and EXPLAINING a strategy, and on flexibility rather than one prescribed method.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): mentally compute 45×8 by partitioning and state the partition used. Tier B (10–11): derive 6.5×4 from a known fact, explaining the derivation. Tier C (11): solve a mixed-operation mental calculation like 250×3 + 500 and justify the strategy and order.
bestPractices: Teach a REPERTOIRE of strategies (partition, compensate, double/halve, derive, factorise) and, crucially, WHEN each is efficient — the goal is flexible choice, not one algorithm done in the head.
Make strategy TALK routine: children explain and compare methods ('I did 40×8 then 5×8; you doubled 45 three times') so efficiency and structure become explicit and shareable.
Use derived-fact chains from a known core fact — from 6×4 reach 60×4, 6.5×4, 12×4 — to show mental maths is about leveraging what you already know, reducing memory load.
Ground partitioning and compensation in place value and the distributive/associative laws so mental methods are understood, not tricks; connect to the area-model and properties work already secured.
Fold in order of operations for mixed strings (250×3 + 500) so children apply BODMAS mentally, and always encourage an estimate to sanity-check the mental result.
keyRepresentations: Partitioning diagrams / bar splits: 45 shown as 40 + 5, each part multiplied then recombined (distributive law made visible).
Empty number line for compensation and doubling/halving jumps (99×6 as 100×6 then back 6).
Derived-fact 'spider' or web from a core fact to its relatives (6×4 → 60×4, 6.5×4, 3×4).
Jottings scaffold — minimal written support for intermediate results in a multi-step mental calculation (not a full written method).
commonMisconceptions: Attempting the formal WRITTEN algorithm in the head (carrying columns mentally) instead of using an efficient mental strategy — error-prone and slow.
Partitioning errors: multiplying only one part (45×8 → 40×8 = 320 and forgetting 5×8) — dropping a partial product.
Compensation without adjusting back (99×6 = 100×6 but forgetting to subtract 6).
Ignoring order of operations in mixed mental strings (doing 250×3+500 left-to-right differently).
Believing there is one 'right' mental method, so failing to pick the most efficient route for the particular numbers.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11, develop flexible mental calculation for multiplication, large numbers and mixed-operation strings. Learners build a repertoire of strategies — partitioning, compensation, doubling/halving, derived facts, factorising — and learn to SELECT and EXPLAIN the most efficient route for the particular numbers, applying order of operations mentally and sanity-checking with estimation. The central objective is flexible, structure-seeking judgement and strategy talk, not running a written column algorithm in the head.

activities.title: Mental maths strategy workspace: split, compensate, derive
feedback: If a partial product is dropped (e.g. answering 320 for 45×8, forgetting 5×8), prompt: say each partial product aloud and add them; jot the parts down if working memory overloads.
If compensation is left unadjusted (99×6 = 600), ask: what did you change about 99, and what must you do to put that back? (Subtract 6 to reach 594.)

If the written column method is attempted mentally and a carry is lost (answer off by tens), suggest partitioning or doubling (45×8 = 45×4×2 = 180×2 = 360) as a carrying-free mental route; reserve columns for paper.
If order of operations is ignored in a mixed string (e.g. computing 250×(3+500)), clarify: multiply before add here — do 250×3 first, then add 500.
If the strategy is sound but a sub-total is miscomputed, do not reteach the strategy: have the learner re-state and recompute the slipped part, then check by estimation.
activities.rationale: Effective mental calculation depends on a repertoire of strategies and efficient choice grounded in place value and properties of operations, rather than mentally running the written algorithm. Making decomposition explicit lets the classic dropped-partial-product error become visible and correctable.
sourceClaims: Pupils use place-value understanding and properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide; flexible mental strategies rest on structure and repeated reasoning.
Effective mental calculation depends on a repertoire of strategies (partitioning, compensation, derived facts) and choosing efficiently, not on mentally running the written algorithm.
learnerActions: Given 45 × 8, partition 45 into 40 and 5, multiply each part by 8 (40×8 = 320, 5×8 = 40), then recombine the partial products to reach 360.
Use compensation on 99 × 6: compute 100 × 6 = 600, then subtract the adjustment 6 to get 594 — stating both the rounding move and the adjust-back step.
Grow a derived-fact chain from a known core fact: from 6 × 4 reach 60 × 4, 6.5 × 4 and 12 × 4, saying how each relative is obtained.
Solve a mixed-operation string such as 250 × 3 + 500: multiply first (250 × 3 = 750), then add 500 to get 1250, stating the order used.
For at least one calculation, try two different strategies (e.g. partitioning vs doubling 45 three times) and judge which was more efficient for those numbers.
Before finalising, give a rough estimate (45 × 8 lies between 40 × 8 = 320 and 50 × 8 = 400, so around 360) and check the answer fits.
activities.intendedInsight: Mental calculation is about decomposing numbers flexibly using place value and the distributive/associative laws, leveraging known facts to reduce memory load, and choosing the route that suits the particular numbers — not visualising a column method.

activities.title: Explain and compare: strategy talk
feedback: Reward reasoning about WHY a route is efficient for these numbers, not just fast answers.
If the learner believes there is one 'right' mental method, present a case where a different strategy is clearly quicker (e.g. 99×6 by compensation vs partitioning) to prompt flexible selection.
When comparing, ask the learner to state the condition that makes each strategy efficient (numbers near a round number favour compensation; even factors favour doubling/halving).
activities.rationale: Strategy talk and comparison help develop flexible mental calculation; explaining and judging which route is more efficient rehearses the efficient-choice reasoning the objective targets. A responsive questioner may prompt this articulation during teaching, though its instructional effect here is proposed rather than independently validated.
sourceClaims: Effective mental calculation depends on a repertoire of strategies (partitioning, compensation, derived facts) and choosing efficiently, not on mentally running the written algorithm.
learnerActions: After solving a calculation mentally, explain aloud how it was worked out ('I did 40×8 then 5×8 and added them').
Compare your method with a different method for the same calculation (e.g. 'you doubled 45 three times') and decide which is more efficient and why.
Respond to prompts such as: 'How did you break up 45 × 8 to make it easier?', 'Could doubling help instead?', and 'In 250 × 3 + 500, which do you do first and why?'
Judge whether a proposed shortcut is valid and efficient for the given numbers, not just whether it reaches an answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating and comparing methods makes efficiency and mathematical structure explicit and shareable, and builds the metacognition behind flexible choice — the real target beyond speed.

activities.title: Strategy reference and fluency practice
feedback: For a missing-partial item, if the blank is filled wrongly, return to the partition and recompute each part separately.
For strategy-matching, if an inefficient strategy is chosen, ask the learner to try both and time or count the steps to feel the difference.
Recognition-only matching confirms identification but does not by itself build the decomposition move; follow with an active calculation the learner performs from scratch.
activities.rationale: Reference material and matching/completion items support fluency and strategy identification; however such formats confirm or check rather than elicit the independent decomposition and recombination that is the core skill, so they should accompany active construction. No cited source directly establishes this affordance distinction.
learnerActions: Consult a worked reference showing partition, compensate and derive each worked once, with a note of when each is most useful, then apply the matching strategy to new calculations.
Complete fill-in-the-missing-partial items (e.g. 40×8 + __ = 360) to confirm all parts are tracked.
Match each calculation to its most efficient strategy and justify the match.
Practise derived-fact chains for fluency, timing optional, always stating the known fact the answer was derived from.
activities.intendedInsight: A reference of worked strategies plus targeted practice consolidates fluency and strategy-identification, provided the learner is actively producing or completing calculations rather than only recognising answers.

constraints: The objective is flexible mental strategy and explanation, not merely obtaining the correct answer; assessment should watch for a deliberate, tracked strategy across steps.

Recognition-only formats (multiple choice, matching) confirm strategy identification and fluency but do not elicit the independent decomposition and recombination that is the core skill; pair them with learner-constructed calculations.
A static strategy poster or worked reference is a useful aid but does not substitute for active practice of mental strategies; use it alongside the learner doing calculations.

Draggable partition tiles, compensation sliders and derived-fact webs are optional ways to externalise the mental move and make a dropped partial visible; they are illustrative, not required mechanisms, and the ultimate aim is for the learner to perform the move in their head.
Jottings are a legitimate minimal scaffold for intermediate results when working memory overloads; they should not become a full written column method, which is a different (paper) competence.
Ground partitioning and compensation in place value and the distributive/associative laws so methods are understood rather than applied as tricks.
Always include an estimate to sanity-check the mental result.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources (CCSS-M 4.NBT and NCETM) were marked verified:false in the source row; treat the mental-strategy repertoire and efficiency claims as reasonable guidance that has not been independently re-checked here.

Arithmetic self-check of the examples: 40×8 = 320 and 5×8 = 40 sum to 360; 45×4×2 = 180×2 = 360; 99×6 via 100×6 = 600 then −6 = 594 (the source gave the method without stating 594, added for completeness); 250×3 = 750 then +500 = 1250. No arithmetic errors found in the source examples.

The original 'parentTitle' was 'Ratio (age 10+)' while the content is mental multiplication/mixed operations — this appears to be a mislabel in the source metadata and does not affect the learning content; the original row field was not altered.

The source asserted that 3D 'adds nothing' and that a static picture 'can't' provide active practice; these have been softened to scoped affordance/objective-limit statements, since comparative necessity is not established by the sources.

Activity 1 (reference and fluency) sourceClaims were set to [] because no sources[].claim directly supports the reference/practice-format affordance principle. The Y6 claim was also removed from activity 0's sourceClaims because it supports the topic rather than that activity's repertoire/decomposition teaching principle.

probeDeeper: How did you break up 45 × 8 to make it easier?
Is there another mental route to 45 × 8 — could doubling help?
In 250 × 3 + 500, which do you do first and why?
Roughly, about how big should 45 × 8 be? Does your answer fit?
assess.correctAnswer: 360 (e.g. 40×8 + 5×8 = 320 + 40; or 45×8 = 45×4×2 = 180×2). 1250 (250×3 = 750, + 500 = 1250). The teacher watches for a deliberate mental strategy — partitioning, doubling, or compensation — held together across steps, not a mentally-visualised column algorithm.

errorPatterns.pattern: partitions but forgets to combine all parts — does 40×8 = 320 and forgets 5×8, answering 320
errorPatterns.nextMove: rehearse holding two parts: say each partial product aloud and add; jot the parts if working memory overloads.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer missing a partial product; child loses track of the second piece

errorPatterns.pattern: attempts the column algorithm mentally and loses carries
errorPatterns.nextMove: teach partitioning/compensation as the mental route (45×8 = 45×4×2), which avoids carrying; reserve columns for paper.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child visualises columns, drops a carry, gives an answer off by tens

errorPatterns.pattern: ignores order of operations in the mixed calculation — does 250×(3+500) or adds before multiplying
errorPatterns.nextMove: clarify multiply before add here; compute 250×3 first, then add 500.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: answer far too large; child combined 3 and 500 first

errorPatterns.pattern: correct strategy, arithmetic slip in a partial step
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach; have the child re-state and recompute the slipped part, then check by estimation.

responseLevels.gap: has no mental strategy, tries columns in the head and loses carries, or mis-orders the mixed calculation.
responseLevels.full: selects an efficient mental strategy (partition, compensate, derive), tracks the parts, respects operation order in the mixed calculation, and sanity-checks by estimation.
responseLevels.partial: partitions or doubles for the multiplication but drops a part, or needs support to sequence the mixed-operation calculation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to do these in their head, saying their strategy aloud: 45 × 8, then 250 × 3 + 500. Watch whether they partition, compensate, or use derived facts — and whether they keep track of the parts mentally rather than reaching for a written method.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The objective is FLEXIBLE mental strategy, not just getting the answer. Watching whether the child partitions/compensates and tracks partial results reveals strategic fluency; a child who tries to 'do the written method in their head' typically loses the carries and stalls — exposing the absence of genuine mental strategies.
